title: Targeted chromosomal sequencing of wild bonobos identifies a genetically distinct subpopulation east of the Lomami river.
journal: Genome Biology (first published 2026-07-21; PMID 42482122; the journal version is NOT in PubMed Central, but the identical preprint is, as PMC12803258)
data_url: Two sources, both of which I opened. (1) ENA (European Nucleotide Archive, the public DNA sequence repository) study PRJEB96168, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/view/PRJEB96168 - this is the entire data availability statement, and it holds ONLY raw sequencing reads: 420 runs, 155 ENA samples, 273,616,360,300 bytes (273.6 GB) of FASTQ, 156 of the 420 runs submitted as BAM+BAI alignment files. (2) Four supplementary files attached to the article, which I downloaded and parsed: MOESM1 (256,714 bytes, tables S1-S5), MOESM2 (4,379,415 bytes, figures PDF), MOESM3 'Metrics_final.xlsx' (716,808 bytes, nine sheets of per-sample laboratory metrics, site labels and GPS coordinates), MOESM4 'Locator_results.xlsx' (10,272 bytes, 29 rows of geolocalisation error in km). No variant-call file (VCF), no genotype matrix, no genotype-likelihood file and no code repository exists anywhere in the deposit.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC returned exactly 1 hit for the DOI (PMID 42482122, Genome Biology, first published 2026-07-21). The journal version is not open in PubMed Central (isOpenAccess 'N', inPMC 'N') and Crossref lists the licence as CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0, so I read the Methods and the data availability statement from the identical preprint, which IS open full text in Europe PMC (PMC12803258). NCBI elink from PubMed to GEO, SRA, BioProject, BioSample and Nucleotide returned zero links for this paper. I downloaded and parsed all four supplementary files myself and counted rows rather than trusting captions. Verified counts: MOESM3 sheet 'MAIN' has 277 non-empty rows of which 169 carry a Sample Identifier, all 169 reading 'QC Pass = Yes', all 169 Pan paniscus, 13 of them with Site Location 'Unknown' (these are the previously published whole-genome blood and cell-line samples), leaving exactly 156 wild samples - the paper's headline number. Sample type across those 169: 96 'Dna from Feces', 60 'Feces', 12 'Blood', 1 'Lymphoblastoid'. Sex is 'U' (unknown) for 141 of 169, female for 22, male for 6. MOESM3 sheet 'Coordinates_known_data' has 156 rows carrying a Sample Identifier, and this is the decisive count: only 75 of those 156 carry a latitude AND longitude, 81 read 'N/A', the 75 collapse to just 57 distinct coordinate pairs, latitude is written in two incompatible formats (54 rows decimal degrees such as 'S2.46726', 21 rows degrees-minutes-seconds such as "S1 09'34""), the hemisphere is a letter prefix rather than a sign, longitude sits in an unnamed sixth column that the header row does not label, and 47 of the 156 rows have no collection date. MOESM4 I reproduced exactly: 29 samples, 6 sites (Kokolopori 13, TL2-E 7, Manzano 3, Lomako 3, TL2-W 2, Ikela 1), median geolocalisation error 53.10 km with same-site samples present (paper says '~53 km'), minimum 5.06 km, maximum 268.00 km - all three match the preprint text to the decimal. I also computed the number the paper does not highlight: with same-site samples removed, median error rises to 232.13 km and maximum to 953.53 km, a 4.4-fold degradation. MOESM1 tables S1-S5 are tiny summary tables (16, 7, 7, 10 and 13 rows) with no per-sample data. For ENA I pulled the full file report for PRJEB96168 and summed it myself: 420 read runs, 155 unique sample accessions, 157 distinct library names, 3,937,302,421 reads, 273,616,360,300 bytes of FASTQ, library strategy 'Targeted-Capture' for all 420. I queried the ENA 'analysis' result type and it returned an empty table, confirming no processed file of any kind was deposited. I opened one sample record (SAMEA119617170) in full: its only geographic attribute is 'Democratic Republic of the Congo', its collection date is 'not applicable', and its alias is the generic string 'Bonobo sample'. The one good piece of news I verified: the ENA 'library_name' field and the submitted BAM filenames carry the laboratory pool identifiers (for example pL893A2), which do join to the supplementary spreadsheet's Pool_Capture column, so a sample-to-site mapping is technically reconstructible. I downloaded no FASTQ and no BAM.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the analysis pipeline, taken from the open preprint: 272 samples collected and 156 retained after a 0.1x coverage and 1 percent human-contamination filter; mean on-target coverage 3.46x; genotype likelihoods produced with ANGSD v0.935; principal components with PCAngsd and ancestry proportions with NgsAdmix on the 156 samples; a separate GATK v4.2.5 variant-calling run restricted to the 29 samples at 5x or more, yielding 660,992 SNPs after removing sites with more than 50 percent missing data; inbreeding with PLINK Fhat3; fixation index (FST, a measure of genetic differentiation between populations) with PLINK2 and ANGSD; divergence times with G-PhoCS; and geolocalisation with Locator, an existing published deep-learning tool. I could not verify any of those intermediate products because none of them - not the 660,992-SNP VCF, not the ANGSD genotype likelihoods, not the PCA coordinates, not the admixture proportions - was deposited. I also never saw the journal version's own data availability statement; I am relying on the preprint's, which names ENA PRJEB96168 and nothing else. The authors' claim that bonobo home ranges span about 5 km, used to argue 53 km is a useful precision, is text-only.

a1_downloadable.note: PASSES on paper, and I confirmed it: ENA study PRJEB96168 is fully open, no login and no access application, and the four supplementary files downloaded without obstruction. But what downloads is 273.6 GB of raw sequencing reads and four small spreadsheets of laboratory quality-control metrics. Nothing in between exists.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: PASSES narrowly, with a caveat I measured. The coarse label is a real column: 'Site Location' is filled for all 156 wild samples. The fine label the project would actually want - latitude and longitude - is present for only 75 of those 156 rows (81 read 'N/A'), collapses to 57 distinct coordinate pairs, is written in two incompatible formats (54 decimal-degree, 21 degrees-minutes-seconds), encodes the hemisphere as a letter prefix instead of a sign, and puts longitude in an unnamed sixth column the header never labels. So the label exists but is half-missing and needs a careful parser.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAILS, and this is the first hard killer. The model inputs for any version of this project are per-individual genotypes or genotype likelihoods at chromosome 21 sites. Not one genotype is deposited. I queried the ENA 'analysis' result type for PRJEB96168 and it returned an empty table: there is no variant-call file, no genotype-likelihood file, no principal-component table and no ancestry-proportion table. The 660,992-SNP matrix the paper's own analyses rest on exists only on the authors' machines. Getting to a feature table therefore means downloading 273.6 GB of reads and rerunning BWA, Picard, BEDTools, ANGSD and GATK yourself - which the project's own rules forbid (no raw sequencing downloads) and a 16 GB laptop cannot do.

a4_units_stated.note: PASSES but is messy, and the mess is the silent-killer kind. The one clean column is MOESM4's 'Average_distance_with_site_in_km', which names its unit. Elsewhere units are implied and formatted inconsistently: coverage is a text string with a comma decimal separator and a trailing letter ('3,69x'), host-DNA percentage is a text string ('1,08%') in one sheet and a decimal in another, and coordinates mix decimal degrees with degrees-minutes-seconds. None of this crashes a parser; it silently produces wrong numbers.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS, decisively, and the unit of analysis is unambiguous here - it is the individual bonobo. I counted 156 wild samples passing quality control, far below the checklist's 400-row floor for classification and its 1,500-row floor for regression. The subset the prediction task actually used is far smaller: exactly 29 samples at 5x coverage or more, spread over 6 sites, with 13 of the 29 from a single site (Kokolopori) and just 1 from Ikela. Only 75 samples anywhere in the deposit carry a coordinate at all, and those 75 collapse to 57 distinct locations.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 273,616,360,300 bytes (273.6 GB) of FASTQ across 420 ENA runs - I summed the file sizes from the ENA file report myself. The supplementary spreadsheets are only 5.4 MB, but they contain no genetic data whatsoever, so they are not a usable working set.
a6_fits_laptop.note: FAILS. To obtain the features you would have to download a quarter of a terabyte of raw reads, realign them to GRCh38 and rerun genotype-likelihood estimation. That is a multi-day compute-cluster job, not a laptop job, and this project's rules explicitly forbid downloading FASTQ, BAM, CRAM or SRA files.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: PASSES, and unusually well - the bookkeeping is the strongest part of this deposit. My own counts: 169 quality-control-passing rows minus 13 'Unknown'-site published samples equals exactly the paper's 156; MOESM4 has exactly 29 rows for the stated 29 samples at 5x or more; and the median, minimum and maximum geolocalisation errors I computed (53.10, 5.06, 268.00 km) match the preprint's stated '~53 km', '5.06 km' and '268 km' to the decimal. One soft mismatch: ENA lists 155 unique sample accessions and 157 distinct library names against 156 samples in the spreadsheet, so the run-to-sample mapping is off by one or two somewhere.

a8_label_provenance.note: PASSES for the label worth using and FAILS for the one the paper advertises. The 75 latitude/longitude values are handheld GPS readings taken in the forest when the faeces were collected - a physical observation, not a model output. But the paper's headline product is the inferred origin of 9 samples of unknown provenance, and those inferred positions are Locator's own predictions, so training anything on them would be distilling Locator with its accuracy as the ceiling. The 'Site Location' label is also field-recorded, but note that 'Eastern/Western/Central' group membership is itself an output of the paper's principal-component and admixture analyses, so predicting the group from the genotypes that defined it would be leakage by construction.

existing_models.name: Locator (Battey, Ralph and Kern, eLife 2020) - a fully connected neural network that predicts a sample's latitude and longitude directly from its genotypes
existing_models.score_and_split: Open source and openly published (eLife 2020, PMC7324158). This is not a competitor to the project - it is the method the paper itself ran, so the ML work is already done by the authors. Published median test errors from the search summary: 16.9 km on Plasmodium (malaria parasite) data, and within about 4.1 generations of dispersal in simulation, running at least an order of magnitude faster than the earlier model-based approach. On this bonobo dataset I reproduced the authors' own numbers from their supplementary file: median 53.10 km across 29 samples with same-site neighbours present, and - the number they do not headline - median 232.13 km and maximum 953.53 km once same-site neighbours are removed, a 4.4-fold degradation that is the honest leave-one-site-out performance.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Retrieved from the search summary: 'Locator requires a high density of SNPs to achieve accurate predictions of geographical origin.' That is precisely the regime this dataset is not in - one chromosome, mean 3.46x coverage, 29 usable individuals.

existing_models.name: GeoGenIE (Bioinformatics Advances 2025, PMC12596584) - a PyTorch multilayer-perceptron model that predicts the geographic provenance of biodiversity samples from genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphisms
existing_models.score_and_split: Open-source Python package. From the search summary it adds automated hyperparameter tuning, geo-genetic outlier detection and data augmentation on top of the Locator idea, and is aimed explicitly at wildlife management, forensics and conservation. No exact error number verified by me - I read search summaries, not the paper body. Its existence means the 'nobody has applied modern ML to genetic geolocalisation' angle is gone: this is a 2025 open, documented, tuned successor to the exact method this paper used.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I did not open the paper body.

existing_models.name: Ape Atlas (Revive & Restore / Universitat Pompeu Fabra, led by Tomas Marques-Bonet) - a continent-wide forensic genomics platform for tracing the origin of confiscated great apes
existing_models.score_and_split: No score verified. This is the single most important C2 finding and it kills the diversity angle outright: from the project's own public description, the platform has already geolocated more than 500 great ape samples across Sierra Leone, Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Cameroon. Marques-Bonet is the last author of the paper under evaluation, so the same group is already running a far larger version of this exact application, and the Revive & Restore Foundation is named in this paper's funding statement.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved beyond the public project description, which frames portable field sequencing and expanded reference panels as the current work.

existing_models.name: Context, not a model: Han et al. bonobo exome study and Takemoto et al. mitochondrial-DNA study (both cited by this paper)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved independently - I know of them only from this paper's own discussion, which states that its two headline findings (a highly differentiated Western population at Manzano, and a distinct population east of the Lomami river) were already reported by an exome study and by mitochondrial DNA respectively. So the biological result is a confirmation rather than a discovery, which further weakens any 'new signal to model' claim.

c2_audit.note: I ran two searches despite the Part A failure, because the state of the field is the second reason to reject and it is cheap to establish. Absence of further results is weak evidence; this list is not exhaustive.

backbone.name: None fits. A DNA language model such as HyenaDNA or Nucleotide Transformer embeds a DNA sequence, but the quantity here is an individual's genotype across a whole chromosome, not a short sequence window, and the prediction target is a map coordinate for the animal rather than a property of a sequence. There is no pretrained population-genetics backbone, and the 29 usable individuals would not support fitting even a linear head.
backbone.hardware: Not assessed - the question is moot because the genotypes needed as inputs are not deposited.
backbone.licence: The article and supplementary files are CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 per Crossref, which is the most restrictive licence I have seen on a Genome Biology paper in this queue: the 'ND' (no derivatives) term is an awkward fit for redistributing a reprocessed version of the supplementary tables. The ENA reads themselves carry no such restriction.

integration.partner_dataset: Not assessed beyond the obvious: the great-ape whole-genome panel of Prado-Martinez et al. 2013 and de Manuel et al. 2016, which the authors already merged in, and the Ape Atlas reference panel, which is not public.
integration.join_key: The laboratory pool identifier (for example pL893A2), which I verified appears both in the ENA 'library_name' field and in the supplementary 'Pool_Capture' column - that join does work. There is no standard identifier of the kind the checklist wants (no UniProt accession, no Ensembl gene, no genomic coordinate of a variant), because no variant was ever deposited.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written in a way that this deposit could answer: the question worth asking is whether a geolocalisation model trained on one African great ape generalises to another, and answering it needs genotype panels from several species, none of which is in this deposit.

controls.positive_control: A good one exists and the authors effectively ran it: a model must place the 24 samples from TL2 Eastern on the east bank of the Lomami river and the 6 from TL2 Western on the west bank, two sites only about 60 km apart but strongly differentiated. A second, trivially learnable control would be to predict a sample's sequencing coverage from its own read data, which must come out near-perfect.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the coordinate labels within site and confirm the error collapses to the distance one would get by always predicting the overall centroid. Also split by site rather than at random - I already computed what that does using the authors' own file, and the median error goes from 53 km to 232 km, which is the single most informative number in the whole deposit.
controls.external_validation: The 13 previously published whole-genome bonobo samples (Prado-Martinez et al. 2013) are a genuine held-out set of different sample type (blood and cell line rather than faeces) - but 9 of them have no known origin, which is exactly why the authors used them as prediction targets rather than as validation. A collection-date column exists for 109 of 156 samples spanning 2006 to 2019, so a temporal split is nominally possible, but with 29 usable individuals it would be meaningless.

honest_claim_h3: Among 29 wild bonobos sequenced on one chromosome at 5x coverage or better from 6 sampling sites in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a neural network can place an individual within a median of 53 km of its true collection point when other animals from the same site are in the training set, and within a median of 232 km when they are not - so the model is mostly recognising which of 6 known sites a sample came from, not locating it on a map.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use an individual bonobo's chromosome 21 genetic variants to predict where in the Congo rainforest it was living.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per animal: its genetic variants along chromosome 21, read out of DNA recovered from a faecal sample found in the forest. I verified the counts, and they are small: 156 animals passed quality control, only 75 of those have a recorded Global Positioning System coordinate, and only 29 have enough sequencing depth for the task the paper actually performed.
plain_idea.predict: Latitude and longitude, or equivalently which of 6 sampling sites the animal belongs to. The true answer is a handheld GPS reading taken by a field researcher at the moment the faeces were collected - a direct physical observation, not another model's guess.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Wildlife-crime investigators and sanctuaries need to know where a confiscated or rescued ape came from before they can release it, and a genetic test would replace guesswork. Even a failure would be informative, by showing how far apart sampling sites must be before genetics can tell them apart at all.

ml_idea: The idea is genuinely appealing and the project is dead anyway; both halves are worth stating. The appeal: predicting an animal's geographic origin from its DNA is a transfer question that cannot produce a useless answer ('how does accuracy decay as the nearest training site gets further away?'), it serves a named user (wildlife-crime forensics and release decisions at sanctuaries), and it is a measurement nobody can make cheaply any other way. Four reasons the files close it off. First and fatally, no genotype of any kind was deposited. I queried the ENA analysis endpoint for PRJEB96168 and it is empty; the 660,992-SNP matrix underlying every figure in the paper lives only on the authors' machines, so the inputs would have to be rebuilt from 273.6 GB of raw reads through BWA, Picard, ANGSD and GATK - forbidden by this project's rules and impossible on a 16 GB laptop. Second, the sample size is 29 where it counts, not 156: 29 animals at 5x coverage or more, across 6 sites, 13 of them from one site and 1 from another, with only 57 distinct coordinate pairs in the whole deposit. Third, the ML has already been done, by these authors, with an existing open tool - Locator - and its open 2025 successor GeoGenIE is tuned, documented and aimed at exactly this use case; worse, the paper's own last author runs Ape Atlas, which has already geolocated over 500 great ape samples. Fourth, I computed the honest version of their headline number from their own supplementary file and it is much weaker than advertised: median error 53.10 km with same-site neighbours in training, but 232.13 km median and 953.53 km maximum once same-site neighbours are removed. That 4.4-fold gap is the whole result - the model is doing nearest-site lookup, and a plain 6-class nearest-site classifier would probably match it, which is the Part I4 'try the dumbest thing first' test failing before the project starts. What is worth keeping is that one number. Recomputing the leave-one-site-out error from MOESM4 took me seconds and is a legitimate one-paragraph comment on the paper, and the same reframing applies to every published genetic-geolocalisation result: report the leave-site-out error, not the leave-one-sample-out error. If the authors later deposit the 660,992-SNP VCF (a file that would be a few hundred megabytes and would fit the laptop easily), the inputs problem disappears - but the 29-individual sample size would still fail A5, so this stays a reject rather than a park.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated for the modelling task, because there is no route from the deposit to a feature table on a laptop. The 273.6 GB figure is not an estimate: I summed the fastq_bytes field across all 420 runs in the ENA file report myself. Realignment and genotype-likelihood estimation on that volume is a compute-cluster job; the authors used 24 to 64 threads. The only timings I can give are for what I did do: downloading and parsing all four supplementary files took under a minute and well under 1 GB of memory.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Two checks, both of which I ran, and together they took about five minutes. (1) Query the ENA analysis endpoint for PRJEB96168 - https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/filereport?accession=PRJEB96168&result=analysis - and see that it returns an empty table, meaning no variant-call file or genotype file was ever deposited and the only thing available is 273.6 GB of raw reads. (2) Open MOESM4 and count the rows: 29 samples over 6 sites, 13 of them from Kokolopori, median error 53.10 km with same-site neighbours and 232.13 km without. Either one kills the project on its own; the first is the hard killer and the second explains why it would not have been worth doing even if the first had passed.

verdict_reason: Three Part A killers fail, all verified in the files rather than read off the abstract. A3 is the hard one: no genotype data of any kind was deposited. The entire data availability statement is ENA study PRJEB96168, and I confirmed by querying ENA directly that it contains 420 raw read runs totalling 273,616,360,300 bytes and zero analysis objects - no variant-call file, no genotype likelihoods, no principal components, no ancestry proportions. The 660,992-SNP matrix every figure in the paper rests on exists only on the authors' machines, so the model inputs would have to be rebuilt from a quarter of a terabyte of reads through BWA, Picard, ANGSD and GATK, which this project's rules forbid and a 16 GB laptop cannot do (A6 fails for the same reason). A5 fails independently and would still fail even if the genotypes appeared tomorrow: the unit of analysis is the individual bonobo, and I counted 156 passing quality control against a 400-row floor for classification, with the subset the prediction task actually used being exactly 29 animals across 6 sites, 13 of them from Kokolopori and 1 from Ikela, and only 75 samples anywhere in the deposit carrying a GPS coordinate (57 distinct coordinate pairs, written in two incompatible formats with longitude in an unnamed column). Beyond Part A, two things would have sunk it anyway. The ML is already done: the authors themselves ran Locator, an open published neural network, its tuned open successor GeoGenIE appeared in 2025, and this paper's own last author runs Ape Atlas, which has already geolocated more than 500 great ape samples - so there is no novel, better or diversity angle left. And I computed the honest version of their headline result from their own supplementary file: median error is 53.10 km only when other animals from the same site are in the training set, and rises to 232.13 km median and 953.53 km maximum when they are removed, meaning the model is performing nearest-site lookup among 6 known sites rather than locating animals on a map. Three things are worth keeping. The deposit's bookkeeping is excellent and I reproduced four of its numbers exactly (156 samples, 29 high-coverage samples, 53.10 km median, 268.00 km maximum), which is more than most papers in this queue manage. That leave-site-out recomputation is a real, cheap, publishable-adjacent observation that generalises to every genetic-geolocalisation paper: report the leave-site-out error, not the leave-one-sample-out error. And the join from ENA 'library_name' to the supplementary 'Pool_Capture' column does work, so if the authors ever deposit the SNP matrix the data would at least be linkable - though at 29 usable individuals it would still be too small to model.
